common_misconceptions.topic: Translating in Latin instead of English
common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates answer Section A comprehension or commentary questions in Latin when the rubric asks for English, costing marks needlessly. The rubric only requires Latin where it is specifically asked for (4-mark and some 6-mark style questions).
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 and Component 2 sections, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates regularly mistake the pluperfect verb form miserat for the adjective miser, so 'Agamemnon had sent' is read as 'wretched Agamemnon'. Pluperfect endings (-erat, -erant) need to be recognised independently of similar-looking words.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 Question 3, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates skip itaque, tamen, tandem, frustra and similar particles in translation. Each carries marks attached to its meaning and so dropping them loses marks even when the surrounding clause is correctly rendered.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 Question 2 commentary, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.topic: Subjunctive in indirect commands and purpose clauses
common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates either confuse indirect commands (ut + subjunctive after a verb of asking/ordering) with purpose clauses, or fail to notice the subjunctive at all and say the action did happen when it was meant to happen. The Ulixes-Achilli persuasion clause in 2025 caught this out widely.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 Question 3, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates regularly write answers using lines or material outside the line reference given. Even excellent points drawn from outside the lemma cannot be credited, costing easy marks particularly in Component 2 and Component 3A style questions.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 2 and Component 3A sections, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.topic: 8-mark style question — quoting Latin and four points
common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates either forget to quote the Latin (only paraphrasing or translating), or make only one or two general points instead of four distinct points each pegged to a Latin word or phrase. Even strong candidates lose easy marks by missing the four-point structure.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2024 and Summer 2025, Component 3A overview, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates list facts about a monument or social practice without analysis, so AO3 marks are unreachable. The paper rewards knowledge and evaluation throughout, so even short-mark answers need to add a point about significance or effect.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025 executive summary and Component 3B, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Many candidates refer to Lesbia as Catullus's wife in essays on Love and Marriage. The biographical and immediate textual context is important — Lesbia was Catullus's mistress, not his spouse, and this affects the reading of fidelity in the poems.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 2 Theme B, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates identify ancillae as genitive or dative singular when the surrounding passage makes it plural nominative. Case identification needs to be done in context, not by surface form alone, especially in Section B grammar questions.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 Question 5, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Candidates fail to spot compounds like eicio from iacio, convenio from venio or auferre from fero and abs. Compound forms with prefix changes need explicit teaching alongside their simple stems.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Component 1 teacher support materials, Knowledge Organiser, eduqas.co.uk (accessed 2026)

student_errors_by_question_type.5 marks — English Passage Comprehension: Candidates cite content from the English passage without explaining why each point answers the question. The mark scheme expects 5 clearly separated points with a brief explanation tying each to the question's focus; long undirected paragraphs score poorly. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2024 and Summer 2025, Component 3A.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Style Analysis: Candidates spot a device (chiasmus, repetition) but do not explain its effect or link it to the question. The successful pattern is quote, translate, link to the question, move on. Where the question asks about effectiveness or impact, the answer must reach beyond identifying the feature. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 2.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Extended Style Analysis: Candidates make fewer than four distinct points or fail to quote the Latin as the rubric demands. Strong answers produce four cleanly separated points, each anchored to a Latin word or phrase with a comment on effect. Content points are creditable up to a maximum of six marks, so at least some points must be linguistic. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2024 and Summer 2025, Component 3A.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Mini-Essay on a Narrative: Candidates write narrative description without paragraph discipline. Each paragraph should make one point of judgement (AO3) supported by demonstrable knowledge of the text (AO2). The English passages of the narrative count as evidence and are often under-used. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2024 and Summer 2025, Component 3A.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Civilisation Evaluative Essay: Strong answers use brief lists of points and sources rather than lengthy plans, reference specific source material from the paper or wider knowledge, and use both supporting and counter arguments. Candidates who simply repeat the question stimulus or list facts without judgement stall in lower bands. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 3B.
student_errors_by_question_type.16 marks — Theme Evaluative Essay: Best answers select around five or six examples from texts and the picture sources, link consistently back to the precise terms of the question and finish with a brief conclusion. Trying to cover every passage prevents sustained argument; the rubric requires at least four examples. Both texts and pictures must be drawn on for the strongest essays. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2024 and Summer 2025, Component 2.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 1 Language is 50 percent of the qualification (100 marks). Section A is 90 percent of the component (comprehension 55 percent, translation 35 percent). Section B (English-Latin or grammar) is only 10 percent — but is the one place AO1 reaches beyond reading.

Component 2 Themes is 30 percent of the qualification (60 marks). One 16-mark extended essay typically appears in each theme, and the 6-mark style questions are the main differentiators between bands.
Component 3 (3A or 3B) is 20 percent of the qualification (40 marks). For 3A the 12-mark mini-essay and the 8-mark style question carry around half the marks between them.

AO weighting across the whole qualification: AO1 50 percent (all in Component 1), AO2 25 percent (texts and sources knowledge), AO3 25 percent (analysis and evaluation). Component 1 is purely AO1; Components 2 and 3 split AO2 and AO3 evenly.

10 percent of AO1 is attributed to the English-Latin translation OR the grammar alternative. Most centres choose grammar (Section B Question 5 in recent sessions), but the English-Latin option has been growing.
Component 2 set-text rotation runs in three-year cycles: 2024-2026 themes are Romans in the Countryside and Love and Marriage; 2027-2029 themes are Heroes and Villains and Come Dine with Me.

Component 3A narrative rotation runs in two-year cycles: 2026-2027 narratives are Livy (Hannibal Crosses the Alps) and Virgil (Hercules and Cacus); provisional 2028-2029 choices are selections from Apuleius (Cupid and Psyche) and Virgil Aeneid 2, 5-6 (Aeneas and Anchises).

Component 3B civilisation topic rotation runs in three-year cycles: 2024-2026 topics are Roman Family Life and The City of Rome; 2027-2029 topics are Slavery in the Roman World and Roman Festivals and Worship.
current_spec_changes: Specification Version 6 (December 2024) added Livy and Virgil narratives for 2026 and 2027 assessment in Component 3A, removed pre-2023 Component 3B topics from Appendix C and added 2027-2029 topics for Component 3B. Source: WJEC Eduqas GCSE Latin Specification Version 6, eduqas.co.uk.

Component 2 themes were rotated by Specification Version 6: 2021-2023 themes have been removed and 2027-2029 themes (Heroes and Villains; Come Dine with Me) have been added. Source: WJEC Eduqas GCSE Latin Specification Version 6, eduqas.co.uk.

Mark Scheme adjustment in Summer 2025: knowledge of erit and mortuus erant was not required for full credit because these forms fall outside the published GCSE specification. This is a useful indicator that examiners will not penalise candidates for forms outside Appendix B. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, eduqas.co.uk.

Component 2 Resource Booklet captions and bullet points accompanying picture sources will NOT appear in the examination room version — students should not rely on rote-learning caption material that will be removed. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Spring 2026 Newsletter, eduqas.co.uk.
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools recommends explicit teaching of disciplinary vocabulary including etymology and morphology — uniquely relevant for Latin, where prefix-stem-ending breakdown unlocks compound verbs (eicio from iacio, convenio from venio) and English derivations. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk, Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report.

EEF retrieval-practice evidence shows that low-stakes regular recall of vocabulary outperforms re-reading. For a 440-word DVL this argues for short daily quizzes rather than dumping the list. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk, retrieval practice blog series (2023-2025).

Cambridge School Classics Project (the body behind the Cambridge Latin Course endorsed by Eduqas) places sentence reading and storyline-driven vocabulary acquisition before formal grammar drill. Practice questions should preserve narrative context rather than presenting words and forms in isolation. Source: Cambridge School Classics Project teacher guides and CLC Book I-V structure, cambridgescp.com.

For the 8-mark style question, modelling four-point paragraphs with explicit quote / paraphrase / effect / link sequencing produces measurable gains — examiner reports flag this technique as the single biggest discriminator. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2024 and Summer 2025, Component 3A.

For Component 3B 12-mark essays, examiners explicitly recommend brief bullet plans over long detailed plans — saving time for the answer itself was credited in 2025 as a positive shift. Source: Eduqas GCSE Latin Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 3B.

Tes practitioner consensus on GCSE classics: literary devices land best when taught alongside concrete examples from the set text rather than as standalone technical terms; technical-term-only answers are penalised when the effect is not explained. Source: tes.com, GCSE Latin teaching resources (style and structure reference only).

gaps: Set-text rotation: this plan covers the 2024-2026 Component 2 themes, 2026-2027 Component 3A narratives, and 2024-2026 Component 3B topics. When the platform passes the 2027 assessment series, lessons in the Component 2 theme units, Narratives unit and Civilisation units will need regeneration against the new rotation (Heroes and Villains / Come Dine with Me; Cupid and Psyche / Aeneas and Anchises; Slavery / Festivals and Worship). The vocabulary, accidence and syntax unit (Component 1) is stable across rotations and does not need rebuilding.

Both Component 2 themes are covered as separate units even though candidates only sit one — this is intentional so students from different centres find their theme. Both Component 3A and Component 3B paths are similarly covered as separate units (one Narratives unit, two Civilisation units) reflecting Route A vs Route B entry.

Component 3A 2028-2029 set texts (Apuleius Cupid and Psyche; Virgil Aeneid 2/5/6) are flagged as provisional in the Spring 2026 newsletter. Final confirmation expected once Eduqas publishes prescribed material later in the 2025-26 academic year.
